claim: The Swiss HIV Cohort Study (SHCS) is a prospective multicenter study with continuing enrollment, aiming to include all people living with HIV in Switzerland since 1988.
source: The SHCS is a prospective multicenter study with continuing enrollment, aiming to include all people living with HIV in Switzerland since 1988.
evidence: Direct statement about the SHCS study design and objectives, representing established knowledge about this cohort.

claim: About half of all people living with HIV as notified to the Swiss health authorities are voluntarily participating in the SHCS.
source: About half of all people living with HIV (PLWH) as notified to the Swiss health authorities are voluntarily participating in the SHCS, and include three-quarters of all PLWH receiving ART in the country (Schoeni-Affolter et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schoeni-Affolter et al., 2010, describing the representativeness of the SHCS cohort.

claim: Three-quarters of all people living with HIV receiving ART in Switzerland are participating in the SHCS.
source: About half of all people living with HIV (PLWH) as notified to the Swiss health authorities are voluntarily participating in the SHCS, and include three-quarters of all PLWH receiving ART in the country (Schoeni-Affolter et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schoeni-Affolter et al., 2010, describing the representativeness of the SHCS cohort.

claim: As of August 2019, the SHCS has a cumulative total of 20,741 patients.
source: As of August 2019, the SHCS has a cumulative total of 20,741 patients.
evidence: Direct statement of the cohort size at a specific time point, representing data from the study.

claim: The SHCS Drug Resistance Database contains HIV sequence data, primarily partial pol gene sequences, used to determine the presence of DRMs in the viral genome.
source: The SHCS Drug Resistance Database contains the HIV sequence data, primarily partial pol gene sequences, used to determine the presence of DRMs in the viral genome (von Wyl et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to von Wyl et al., 2007, describing the database content and purpose.

claim: The SHCS Drug Resistance Database currently covers 13,798 patients.
source: This data, currently covering 13,798 patients, was obtained from both routine clinical testing and systematic retroactive sequencing of stored plasma samples (Kletenkov et al., 2017; von Wyl et al., 2016).
evidence: Direct statement of the number of patients with resistance data, representing data from the study.

claim: Drug resistance data was obtained from both routine clinical testing and systematic retroactive sequencing of stored plasma samples.
source: This data, currently covering 13,798 patients, was obtained from both routine clinical testing and systematic retroactive sequencing of stored plasma samples (Kletenkov et al., 2017; von Wyl et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kletenkov et al., 2017 and von Wyl et al., 2016, describing the data collection methods.

claim: Only DRMs as defined by the Stanford Drug Resistance Database were considered in the study.
source: To reduce the scope of our systematic screening to only HIV mutations relevant to drug resistance (thus reducing the risk of overtesting), we only considered the presence of DRMs as defined by the Stanford Drug Resistance Database (Rhee et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rhee et al., 2003, describing the use of a standardized definition of DRMs.

claim: Only sequences in ART-naïve individuals (before ART treatment) were considered to avoid confounding by the effect of ART.
source: To avoid confounding by the effect of ART, we only considered sequences in ART-naïve individuals (before ART treatment).
evidence: Direct statement of the study design decision to exclude treated individuals, representing a methodological choice based on inference about confounding.

claim: Data on the HLA class I type was available for 6453 SHCS patients.
source: Data on the HLA class I type was available for 6453 SHCS patients.
evidence: Direct statement of the number of patients with HLA data, representing data from the study.

claim: HLA information was obtained from SNP genotype data, using SNP2HLA with the type 1 Diabetes Genetics Consortium reference panel for HLA imputation techniques on the exome/SNP data.
source: This information was obtained from SNP genotype data, using SNP2HLA with the type 1 Diabetes Genetics Consortium reference panel for HLA imputation techniques on the exome/SNP data (Jia et al., 2013; Szolek et al., 2014; Dilthey et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jia et al., 2013; Szolek et al., 2014; Dilthey et al., 2016, describing the HLA imputation methodology.

claim: The analyses were limited to HLA class I (HLA-A, -B, and -C) considering the existing literature supporting the role of HLA class I peptides in HIV control.
source: We limited our analyses to that of the HLA class I (HLA-A, -B, and -C) considering the existing literature supporting the role of HLA class I peptides in HIV control (Leslie et al., 2010; Pereyra et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Leslie et al., 2010 and Pereyra et al., 2010, describing the rationale for focusing on HLA class I.

claim: Of the 6453 patients with HLA data, 3997 additionally had drug resistance testing data.
source: Of these patients with HLA data, 3997 additionally had drug resistance testing data.
evidence: Direct statement of the number of patients with both HLA and resistance data, representing data from the study.

claim: There were 5561 possible combinations of DRMs and HLA-I types represented in the dataset.
source: As there were a possible 5561 combinations represented in our dataset, it was necessary to reduce these candidate pairs to only those for which our data provided sufficient statistical power to detect an association (Figure 1).
evidence: Direct statement of the number of possible combinations, representing data from the study and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Combinations were filtered to only those where the number of SHCS patients with the given mutation or HLA type were sufficient to provide a statistical power of 0.8, assuming an odds ratio of 3.
source: To do this, we filtered out only the combinations where the number of SHCS patients with the given mutation or HLA type were sufficient to provide a statistical power of 0.8, assuming an odds ratio (OR) of 3.
evidence: Direct statement of the filtering criteria based on statistical power calculations, representing a methodological decision.

claim: After filtering for statistical power, 225 DRM:HLA pairs remained for analysis.
source: This resulted in 225 pairs, from which 225 logistic regression models were made.
evidence: Direct statement of the number of pairs analyzed, representing data from the study and shown in Figure 1.

claim: A Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment was used to account for multiple testing, considering a false discovery rate of 0.2.
source: We then used a Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment to account for multiple testing, considering a false discovery rate of 0.2.
evidence: Direct statement of the multiple testing correction method and threshold, representing a methodological decision.

claim: Three DRM:HLA pairs were found to have a significant impact of the queried HLA type on the odds of observing the DRM after multiple testing adjustment.
source: Using logistic regression models, we found three DRM:HLA pairs after multiple testing adjustment (described in Supplementary file 1), with a significant impact of the queried HLA type on the odds of observing the DRM: RT-E138:HLA-B18 (OR 6.999, 95% CI 4.662–10.413), RT-E138:HLA-A24 (OR 2.444, 95% CI 1.602–3.658), and RT-V179:HLA-B35 (OR 2.431, 95% CI 1.398–4.108).
evidence: Direct statement of the results from logistic regression models with specific odds ratios and confidence intervals, representing data from the study.

claim: RT-E138:HLA-B18 has an odds ratio of 6.999 (95% CI 4.662–10.413) for the association between HLA-B18 and RT-E138 mutation.
evidence: Direct statement of the odds ratio from logistic regression analysis, representing data from the study.

claim: RT-E138:HLA-A24 has an odds ratio of 2.444 (95% CI 1.602–3.658) for the association between HLA-A24 and RT-E138 mutation.
evidence: Direct statement of the odds ratio from logistic regression analysis, representing data from the study.

claim: RT-V179:HLA-B35 has an odds ratio of 2.431 (95% CI 1.398–4.108) for the association between HLA-B35 and RT-V179 mutation.
evidence: Direct statement of the odds ratio from logistic regression analysis, representing data from the study.

claim: All three significant DRM:HLA combinations involved a DRM in the reverse transcriptase (RT) gene.
source: All three combinations involved a DRM in the reverse transcriptase (RT) gene.

claim: Of the three significant combinations, two were with HLA-B, while one was with HLA-A.
